source: Wikipedia: Herman Kahn
finding: Kahn joined RAND as a mathematician, studied nuclear war survivability, and wrote future-as-story scenarios. He founded the Hudson Institute in 1961.
numbers: Born 1922, died 1983. On Thermonuclear War (1960) sold 14,000 copies in two months. Escalation ladder: 16 steps in 1962, 44 steps by 1965. Hudson Institute founded 1961.
limits: Encyclopedia page, not the primary books. Kahn scenarios were narrative and war-game based, not tested for forecast accuracy.
agent_relevance: Scenarios as stories from inside a future is the oldest form. An agent can write a story per branch, but the tradition gives no accuracy test.

source: Kahn and Wiener (1967) The Year 2000 (as described on Wikipedia)
finding: The Year 2000 listed 100 technical innovations judged very likely in the last third of the 20th century, next to branching baseline scenarios.
numbers: Table of 100 innovations. First ten include lasers, strong materials, new aircraft types, better weather forecasting, new power sources. Predicted Japan above the US in per-capita income by 1990 (called controversial).
limits: Only the Wikipedia summary was read. No hit-rate count of the 100 items was found this session.
agent_relevance: A long list of single predictions mixed with scenarios. Our agent should score list items separately from story branches.

source: Wikipedia: Scenario planning
finding: Kahn (RAND, 1950s) wrote stories from inside the future. Berger in France built La Prospective with normative scenarios at the same time. Wack at Shell (from 1971) turned scenarios into a strategy tool, pushed on by the 1973 oil shock.
numbers: Kahn books: Thinking About the Unthinkable (1962 per the Kahn page; 1965 per this page), The Year 2000 (1967). Berger book 1964. Diffenbach 1983 survey: alternate scenarios were the 3rd most popular long-range technique, used by 68 percent of large firms.
limits: Page says evidence for value is largely anecdotal and mostly from Shell. Dates conflict between pages for one Kahn book.
agent_relevance: Three lineages (Kahn, Berger, Wack) have three goals: explore, steer, change mental models. The agent should state which goal a scenario set serves.

source: Wikipedia: Scenario planning (Shell audit claim)
finding: An early-1980s review by de Geus's team reportedly found weak strategy implementation was caused by decision-making after the scenarios, not the scenarios themselves.
numbers: Shell analysts claimed planning helped make the company the largest in the world (Schwartz 1991).
limits: Self-report by the firm; no control group; survivorship risk.
agent_relevance: Scenario value depends on the step from scenario to decision. The scaffold should force a decision test after each scenario set.

source: Wikipedia: Pierre Wack
finding: Wack is credited with first using scenarios in private-sector planning at Shell London in the 1970s. His two 1985 HBR articles carried Kahn's ideas into business strategy. The page claims scenarios let Shell anticipate two oil shocks.
numbers: Two HBR articles (1985): Uncharted Waters Ahead; Shooting the Rapids. Chermack 2017 biography.
limits: The two-shock claim needs a citation; the Wack articles were not opened.
agent_relevance: Wack aims to change the manager's mental model, not to predict. A different success metric from forecasting.

source: Ritchey (2006) General Morphological Analysis: a general method for non-quantified modelling (adapted from Ritchey 1998)
finding: GMA builds a Zwicky box: list parameters, give each a set of values, and treat each combination as a configuration. Cross-consistency assessment then removes pairs of values that cannot co-exist, leaving a solution space.
numbers: Example box 5x5x3 = 75 cells. Swedish shelter-policy field 4x4x4x3x3x4 = 2,304 configurations (the original 10-parameter field had over 500,000). A field of 100,000 configurations needs only a few hundred pairwise judgments. Fig 3 marks 15 pair relations. Over 100 computer-aided projects since 1995.
quote: Examining all possible configurations would take a good deal more time and effort.
limits: Written by the method's main advocate. Judgments are human; group trials are described but no inter-rater numbers are given.
agent_relevance: Direct fit for an operator: build a box, check pairs, keep consistent cells. Pair checks grow quadratically while configurations grow exponentially, so an LLM can do them cheaply.

source: Ritchey (2006) GMA, three kinds of inconsistency
finding: CCA allows logical contradictions, empirical implausibility and normative constraints, and says normative judgments must not enter first.
numbers: Three types; normative judgments held back until the possible set is found. Identical fields were given to different groups and the results compared.
limits: Reproducibility claim is described, not quantified.
agent_relevance: Order of checks: logic, then evidence, then values. Matches a guardrail to keep facts and preferences apart.

source: Ritchey (2006) GMA, Zwicky's principle
finding: Zwicky generalised morphology from anatomy and geology to relations among concepts and ideas. He called it totality research and worked on it about 30 years, from the 1940s to 1974.
numbers: Zwicky 1966 p.34 quote; Zwicky 1969 book Discovery, Invention, Research; the field can have any number of dimensions, not just 3.
quote: nothing can be discarded a priori as being unimportant.
limits: Historical account by Ritchey, not Zwicky's own tests of the method.
agent_relevance: Origin of the exhaustive-enumeration idea: list the space first, prune later.

source: Wikipedia: Morphological analysis (problem-solving)
finding: Morphological analysis suits multi-dimensional problems that cannot be quantified and where causal models and simulation work poorly. CCA removes illogical combinations rather than reducing variables.
numbers: Used in engineering design, technology forecasting, organisation design, policy analysis. Ritchey 1998, 2006, 2011; Alvarez and Ritchey 2015.
limits: No accuracy studies are given.
agent_relevance: Use where numbers are missing; do not use where a simple model exists.

source: Wikipedia: Delphi method
finding: Delphi was developed at RAND by Helmer, Dalkey and Rescher, after a 1944 US Army Air Corps report on future military technology. The authors disliked the name for sounding occult.
numbers: Gordon and Helmer 1964 report. Basu and Schroeder (1977): 3 to 4 percent error on two-year sales, versus 10 to 15 percent for quantitative methods and about 20 percent for unstructured forecasts. Fast-track Delphi about 3 weeks. eLAC Delphi: 5 rounds, 1,454 contributions. TechCast: 100 experts.
limits: Page calls the overall track record mixed; the sales figure is one case. Consensus is not proof of truth.
agent_relevance: The Delphi loop (independent answer, anonymous feedback, revise) is a ready template for an LLM panel.

source: Wikipedia: Delphi method, variants and critiques
finding: Variants: real-time, Policy Delphi (desirability, feasibility, probability scales), Argument Delphi (Kuusi), Disaggregative Policy Delphi (Tapio; clusters build scenarios in the last round), Hyperdelphi, fast-track.
numbers: Critiques: strong personalities may dominate; self-rated expertise weighting may encourage overconfidence; panelists without expertise only add confidence to ignorance; cross-impact analysis was added to handle multi-factor forecasts.
limits: Secondary description; Sackman 1974 and Rowe and Wright were cited there but not read.
agent_relevance: Disaggregative Policy Delphi links Delphi to scenarios directly: cluster the answers into scenario groups. A useful operator.

source: Dalkey and Helmer (1962) An Experimental Application of the Delphi Method to the Use of Experts, RAND RM-727/1
finding: The founding Delphi experiment is an abridged revision of a report on using experts, part of RAND's internal Project Delphi.
numbers: 24 pages, 1962. Only the catalogue page was read; no respondent or round figures.
limits: Full PDF returned 403, so no numbers were read. Do not cite numbers from it.
agent_relevance: Founding paper; its numbers must be fetched by another route.

source: Wikipedia: Cross-impact analysis (Gordon and Helmer 1966)
finding: Cross-impact analysis gives each event an initial probability and a conditional probability for each pair, then runs simulations to produce scenarios.
numbers: Event set of 10 to 40 events. First form was a card game, Future, programmed at UCLA in 1968. Institute for the Future added time series in 1972. Delphi plus cross-impact combined in 1984.
limits: Needs exact probabilities and can produce impossible values with negative impacts. Intelligence versions use plus/minus ratings and are harder to reproduce.
agent_relevance: A pairwise event-link scheme close to CCA but with probabilities. The agent must check the conditionals for coherence.

source: Wikipedia: Stress test (financial)
finding: Large banks began internal stress tests in the early 1990s; a 1996 Basel I amendment required them; regulators began their own tests after 2007. Scenarios are only as good as the designers' imagination.
numbers: EBA 2009 and 2010 adverse scenario: euro-area growth -0.6 percent; revised to -4.0 percent for 2011. 25 banks failed the 2014 EBA test. US rule from Oct 2012: twice-yearly tests of the largest banks; from 2014 banks with $10 to 50 billion in assets.
limits: Secondary source. Taleb: arbitrary-number tests can be gamed. A Saxo Bank economist called the EBA tests a walk in the park.
agent_relevance: Scenario severity is chosen by people; groupthink hides plausible futures. The agent needs a rule for how severe a stress is and who sets it.

source: Federal Reserve (2009) The Supervisory Capital Assessment Program: Design and Implementation
finding: SCAP stress-tested the 19 largest US bank holding companies under two scenarios: a consensus baseline and a more adverse one that is explicitly not a worst case but severe and plausible.
numbers: 19 BHCs hold two-thirds of assets and over half of loans. Baseline = average of Consensus Forecasts, Blue Chip and SPF (Feb 2009). Adverse scenario probability anchors: about 10 percent chance of 2010 unemployment this high (Blue Chip history); about 15 percent joint GDP and unemployment (survey subjective probabilities). Adverse path: 2010 unemployment 10.3 percent; GDP -3.3 percent in 2009 and +0.5 percent in 2010. Horizon two years.
limits: Authors admit forecasts moved: consensus for 2010 unemployment was 9.3 percent by results time. Excludes about $400 billion of losses already taken.
agent_relevance: A scenario with a stated probability anchor (10 to 15 percent) is a pattern the agent can copy: say how likely the stress is and how that was derived.

source: Federal Reserve (2009) SCAP Overview of Results (May 7, 2009)
finding: Under the more adverse scenario, two-year losses at the 19 firms were put at about $600 billion; 10 of 19 firms needed more capital, $185 billion in all.
numbers: Losses $600 billion (loans about $455 billion; trading and securities $135 billion; consumer and residential loans $322 billion, 70 percent of loan losses). Tier 1 capital about $835 billion at Q4 2008. 10 of 19 short, 9 adequate. Buffer need $185 billion, or $75 billion after Q1 revenue. Treasury preferred equity: $216 billion.
limits: Supervisory estimates, not realised outcomes. One common scenario applied to all firms.
agent_relevance: A scenario whose output is a decision number (capital) and a pass or fail per firm is a model of scenario-to-action.

source: Borio, Drehmann and Tsatsaronis (2014) Stress-testing macro stress testing: does it live up to expectations? BIS WP 369
finding: Macro stress tests are poor early-warning devices in calm times, work for crisis management and resolution, and have indirect benefits for thinking about financial stability.
numbers: No numbers in the abstract.
limits: Only the abstract page was read, not the full paper.
agent_relevance: The weak point is predicting before a crisis. The agent should not trust a scenario set to flag a rare event it has no data on.

source: Csaszar, Peterson and Wilde (2026) The Strategic Foresight of LLMs: Evidence from a Fully Prospective Venture Tournament
finding: On 30 live Kickstarter tech ventures, frontier LLMs ranked fundraising outcomes better than 346 experienced managers and 3 MBA investors.
numbers: 870 pairwise comparisons per model. Spearman: Gemini 2.5 Pro 0.74; GPT-5 family 0.67-0.71; best expert 0.45; Prolific crowd 0.19; human range 0.04-0.45. Gemini vs Expert 3: diff 0.29 (p=0.063); vs Prolific 0.55 (p=0.001). 20 LLMs, temperature 0.5.
limits: Only 30 projects; one platform; 3 investors. Claude models ranked near the bottom of the LLMs. Size did not predict: Gemma-3-4b beat 27b.
agent_relevance: Evidence that LLMs can rank strategic outcomes from documents. Pairwise ranking is a cheap, scoreable form.

source: Csaszar et al. (2026) ensembles and replication
finding: Averaging models or adding humans did not beat the best single model. A preregistered replication on a second sample gave similar patterns.
numbers: Best human + Gemini 2.5 Pro: rho 0.67 (below 0.74). Gemini + GPT-5 Mini: 0.77 (+0.03, not significant). Frontier trio, all 20 LLMs, human-only and grand ensembles all below the best model. Replication: 26 projects (3 removed); model rank order correlated about 0.54 across 19 models; 30.8 percent of projects raised under $100.
limits: Ensembles were ex post aggregations; interactive human-AI work not tested. Replication was LLM-only.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a crowd or panel beats picking the best method; test it.

source: Csaszar et al. (2026) model structure results
finding: Model family and reasoning mode had inconsistent effects. Models within a family correlate strongly, so a same-family panel adds little independent signal.
numbers: GPT-5 variants inter-correlate 0.80-0.97; GPT-5-Nano only 0.44-0.65 with siblings and scored worse. Expert-to-top-LLM correlations about 0.2-0.58. Grok-4 reasoning beat non-reasoning; DeepSeek Chat beat DeepSeek Reasoner.
limits: Single task, single period.
agent_relevance: Panels should span families, not copies of one model (links to the correlated-errors guardrail).

source: Lorenz and Fritz (2026) Scalable Delphi: Large Language Models for Structured Risk Estimation
finding: Scalable Delphi runs a panel of LLM personas through Delphi rounds with an LLM mediator giving anonymous summary feedback. Estimates correlated strongly with ground truth on three cyber benchmarks.
numbers: Pearson r 0.91-0.98 on BountyBench, Cybench, CyberGym (GPT-5.1 and Opus-4.1). Panels of 5 personas. Plausibility ranges held the truth in 39-80 percent of cases. A three-round human Delphi takes 3-4 months (Gordon 2009).
limits: Latent quantities have no ground truth; checks use proxies. Largest gaps to humans on long-horizon and count questions.
agent_relevance: Closest published LLM Delphi with measured accuracy. Persona panel plus mediator is a reusable operator.

source: Lorenz and Fritz (2026) Scalable Delphi, evidence sensitivity
finding: With benchmark and agent identity hidden, panel estimates were noise; correlation rose as evidence was added.
numbers: Anonymised baseline r=0.30 on BountyBench; other benchmarks -0.22 and -0.40 when anonymised; r=0.97 and 0.92 once benchmark and agent info were supplied.
limits: Shows the panel needs real evidence; persona talk alone adds no accuracy.
agent_relevance: A guardrail test: an estimate that does not change with evidence is not trusted.

source: Lorenz and Fritz (2026) Scalable Delphi, replication of human panels
finding: The LLM panels reproduced three published human elicitations on most quantities; divergence came from an ambiguous target and long horizons.
numbers: Ransomware: mean absolute difference to one human panel 16.6 pp; GPT-5.1 within 6 percent of the human median at each tier once the quantity was stated. Sea-level replication of Bamber 2019: human n=14, GPT-5.1 n=14 panels; new evidence shifted GPT-5.1 medians down 11-28 percent. Persona effect 2.4 pp per task vs model effect 4.8 pp; persona-set swap 3.0 pp MAD.
limits: Estimates depend more on the base model than on the persona. LLM rationales are longer: 736 chars (GPT), 414 (Opus), 234 (humans).
agent_relevance: Persona diversity is weaker than model diversity; mix base models.

source: Lorenz and Fritz (2026) Scalable Delphi, rationale analysis
finding: LLM panelists cite the panel mean far more often than humans do, a sign of conformity pressure written into the text.
numbers: Cites panel mean or feedback: humans 0.6 percent; GPT-5.1 +45.4 points; Opus +49.4. Mean over 11 reasoning patterns: humans 16.9 percent, GPT +26.4, Opus +8.8.
limits: The patterns explain only about 2 percent of variance beyond panel and task effects.
agent_relevance: Feedback rounds can drive herding. Keep a first-round independent answer and record it.

source: Bertolotti and Mari (2025) An LLM-Based Delphi Study to Predict GenAI Evolution
finding: An agent system of LLM experts (random nationality, training, field) and a mediator ran five Delphi rounds on GenAI futures, repeated three times.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini, temperature 0.7, 5 rounds, 3 repeats. Themes: geopolitics, economic gaps, regulation, ethics.
limits: No accuracy test against outcomes. Authors list knowledge cutoff, bias and sensitivity to initial conditions as limits. Run-to-run stability not measured.
agent_relevance: Cheap Delphi with no fatigue or bandwagon, but nothing shows the results are correct. Treat as idea generation.

source: Sela (2026) Preserving Disagreement: Architectural Heterogeneity and Coherence Validation in Multi-Agent Policy Simulation
finding: In LLM deliberation with no right answer, panels converge on one option. A different 7-9B model per value perspective cut that convergence; Delphi-style peer exposure made it worse.
numbers: 120 deliberations, two scenarios. First-choice share: child welfare 70.9 to 46.1 percent (p<0.001, r=0.58); housing 46.0 to 22.9 percent (p<0.001, r=0.50). Coherence check lowered concentration 46.1 to 40.8 percent (p=0.004) on one scenario. About half of value conflicts were trustworthy. Three Delphi designs failed (v6.0 peer exposure, v6.1, v7); two rounds of exposure compounded sycophantic flips.
limits: Small 7-9B models; two scenarios; coherence judged by a frontier model (possible confound).
agent_relevance: Classic Delphi feedback hurts when the aim is to keep disagreement. For scenarios, keep branches apart and force model diversity.

source: arXiv search: LLM plus scenario planning plus morphological analysis
finding: An arXiv search for LLM plus morphological analysis and scenario planning returned no on-topic paper.
numbers: One search page: 1 result, unrelated (HYPERmotion robotics). A web search also surfaced an AIES 2024 generative scenario-writing paper, but that page was blocked and not read.
limits: Absence on one search is weak evidence. API rate limits stopped arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex queries.
agent_relevance: Gap: no measured test of LLM-run GMA or Kahn-style scenarios, so our own test would be new.
